title: Green Tea vs Black Tea: Differences and Caffeine
h1: Green tea vs black tea: what's actually different?
meta_description: Green tea and black tea come from the same plant but are processed differently. Compare caffeine, flavor, antioxidants, and brewing technique for both.
body_html:
Every cup of green tea and black tea begins with the same plant: Camellia sinensis. The difference is what happens after the leaves are picked.

Side-by-side comparison

PropertyGreen teaBlack tea
Source plantCamellia sinensisCamellia sinensis
OxidationNone — heated to stop itFull
Caffeine (8oz)~30–50 mg~40–70 mg
Key compoundsEGCG, catechins, L-theanineTheaflavins, thearubigins
FlavorFresh, grassy, vegetalMalty, robust, brisk
Liquor colorPale green-yellowAmber-red
Brew temp74–85°C (165–185°F)91–100°C (195–212°F)
Brew time~1 min (Japanese) or 3–4 min (Western)3–5 min

Processing: oxidation is the dividing line

Black tea is fully oxidized — leaves are bruised, exposed to oxygen, and allowed to turn dark before drying. The reaction develops the malty, robust flavors and the deeper amber color in your cup.

Green tea skips oxidation entirely. Leaves are heated soon after picking (steamed in Japan, pan-fired in China) to deactivate the enzymes that would otherwise turn them brown. The result: a fresher, vegetal cup that retains more of the leaf's original chlorophyll and catechins.

Caffeine

  • Green tea: ~30–50 mg per 8oz cup
  • Black tea: ~40–70 mg per 8oz cup
  • Coffee (for reference): ~95 mg per 8oz cup

Flavor profile

Green tea ranges from grassy and oceanic (Japanese sencha) to nutty and toasty (Chinese longjing). Black tea ranges from malty (Assam) to floral (Darjeeling) to brisk and citrusy (Ceylon).

Health benefits

Both teas contain polyphenols. Green tea is highest in EGCG, a catechin that has been studied in cardiovascular and metabolic research. Black tea's oxidation converts catechins into theaflavins and thearubigins — different compounds that have been studied separately, including in cholesterol research.

How to brew each

Green tea

  • Water: 74–85°C (165–185°F)
  • Time: ~1 minute by Japanese convention (Tea Association of the USA; Ippodo), or 3–4 minutes by general Western guidance (Healthline)
  • Why lower temp: prevents the catechins from turning bitter

Black tea

  • Water: 91–100°C (195–212°F)
  • Time: 3–5 minutes
  • Why hotter: needed to fully extract the oxidized compounds

The first treatise on tea

Lu Yu's Cha Jing (茶經, 760 CE) — the world's first book devoted entirely to tea — already understood that what happens to a leaf after picking changes what the cup does. Tang dynasty tea drinkers separated tea types by processing because the medicinal profiles differed. They had no name for catechin oxidation; they had a thousand years of empirical observation.

What chromatography sees

Modern analysis confirms the split. Green tea preserves EGCG, studied for cardiovascular risk factors in a 55-RCT meta-analysis; black tea's full oxidation converts catechins into theaflavins — a 240-person RCT measured a ~16% LDL reduction over 12 weeks, though the trial tested a theaflavin-enriched extract rather than brewed black tea itself. Same plant, two different chemistries — exactly as the Cha Jing implied.

Steeping Parameters

Green tea is typically steeped at a temperature of 165-185°F, while black tea is often steeped at a higher temperature of 195-212°F.

Steeping Time

The steeping time also differs between the two: green tea is steeped for about 1 minute by Japanese convention, or 3-4 minutes by general Western guidance, while black tea is steeped for 3-5 minutes.

Active Compounds

Research suggests that green tea generally contains a higher amount of L-theanine compared to black tea, which may contribute to its unique characteristics and potential health effects.

This describes published research and general information, not medical or dietary advice.

faqs.q: Which has more caffeine, green tea or black tea?
faqs.a: Black tea typically has more caffeine per cup (40–70mg vs 30–50mg), but matcha — a powdered green tea where you consume the whole leaf — can exceed both at 60–80mg.

faqs.q: Is green tea healthier than black tea?
faqs.a: Both are healthy. Green tea has more EGCG; black tea has more theaflavins. The 'best' tea is the one you'll actually drink consistently.

faqs.q: Can you make black tea from green tea leaves?
faqs.a: Not at home. Once green tea is heat-fixed, the enzymes needed for oxidation are destroyed. Black tea must be made from fresh, unprocessed leaves.
